Furthermore, SCOPS determined that the venture capital fonding does not qualify as a prize or award
consistent with the regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(]) and referenced a 1998 Havard
Business Review article. Specifically, SCOPS concluded:
... [P]ublicly available records indicate that venture capital fonding is an exchange of
value between your company and the venture capitalist. Specifically, venture capital
firms provided you the fonding in exchange for an equity share in your company.
However, a prize or award does not typically consist of an exchange between parties;
rather it is generally an honor that one party gives to another without reciprocal
obligation. Your receipt of such venture fonding in and of itself many not constitute
an award without evidence to demonstrate the fonding was "awarded" for excellence
in the field.
We generally agree with SCOPS that the Petitioner did not establish the Petitioner's receipt of venture
capital fonding qualifies as a prize or award. Although the Petitioner submitted background
information about venture capital fonding, including the importance, criteria, and trends, it did not
demonstrate how the evidence establishes that venture capital fonding is viewed as a prize or an award
rather than an investment or business transaction. Again, venture capital fonding reflects a business
transaction between the investor and the business; the investor does not bestow a type of honor on the
business recognizing an accomplishment or achievement. The investor usually provides fonding with
the intent of making a profit from the business's activities but also risks losing some or all of the
investment. Here, the Petitioner did not show that the venture capital fonding resulted in prizes or
awards from the investors rather than business investments and transactions between the two parties.
Notwithstanding the above, the Petitioner did not establish that any of its venture capital fonding is
nationally or internationally recognized for excellence in the field. Besides the above-mentioned joint
letter from T-M- and A-K-, the Petitioner did not submit any independent, objective evidence showing
that the particular capital venture fonding from T-M-, A-K-, or any other investors is nationally or
internationally recognized for excellence in the field. Furthermore, although the Petitioner offered

national or international recognition for excellence of its venture capital fonding.
For all these reasons, the Petitioner did not demonstrate the Beneficiary meets this criterion.

B. Memberships
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2( o) (3 )(iii)(B)(2) requires "[d ]ocumentation ofthe alien's membership
in associations in the field for which classification is sought, which require outstanding achievements of
their members, as judged by recognized national or international experts in their disciplines or fields."
USCIS determines ifthe association for which the person claims present or past membership requires that
members have outstanding achievements in the field as judged by recognized experts in the field. 3
3 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
3
The Petitioner claims the Beneficiary's eligibility for this criterion based on membership with YC and
references a letter from J-F-, general partner at YC, who stated:
[YC] is an elite network of entrepreneurs and the application process for acceptance is
extremely competitive. In a recent application batch, over 27,000 applications were
received, and only 260 companies were accepted as members, a less than 1% acceptance
rate. Since 2005, [YC] has accepted over 5,000 companies into its network. The
combined value of [YC] companies is over $600B.
Similar to one of the issues discussed under the awards criterion, the Petitioner did not demonstrate the
Beneficiary's membership with YC. Again, the regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(2) requires
"[d ]ocumentation ofthe alien 's membership" (e mphasis added). According to J-F-' s letter, "companies"
receive membership rather than individuals. Although J-F- indicates that "[the Beneficiary] and his co­
founding team were accepted into the YC program," the letter reflects company membership.
Regardless, J-F- also stated that "[b ]ecause ofthe sheer volume of applications, founders must be able to
clearly express why they and their businesses stand out, with characteristics like a formidable founding
team, a clear value proposition, a distinctive contribution within a high-value target market, and
exceptional potential economic value." The petitioner must show that membership in the association
requires outstanding achievements in the field for which classification is sought. 4 Here, J-F-'s letter
discussed the requirements for potential or prospective benefits rather than a determination of past
outstanding achievements. While J-F- claimed that YC has a 1% acceptance rate, the Petitioner did not
establish that membership with YC requires outstanding achievements of it members rather than how
financially successful YC believes that the company might be at some time in the future.
Moreover, the regulation requires membership to be 'judged by recognized national or international
experts in their disciplines or fields." 5 Although J-F- named two other individuals and their companies,
along with himself, who review the applications, the Petitioner did not provide independent, objective
evidence establishing that these individuals qualify as recognized national or international experts.
Accordingly, the Petitioner did not show the Beneficiary fulfills this criterion.

C. Published Materials
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(3) requires "[p]ublished material in professional or
major trade publications or major media about the alien, relating to the alien's work in the field for
which classification is sought, which shall include the title, date, and author of such published material,
and any necessary translation." USCIS first determines whether the published material was related to
the person and the person's specific work in the field for which classification is sought. 6 USCIS then
determines whether the publication qualifies as a professional publication, major trade publication, or
major media publication. 7
4 See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
5 See also generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
6 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
7 Id.
4
The record contains two articles posted on physiciansweekly.com and healthcare.com referencing the
findings of a study from an article co-authored by the Beneficiary. Published material that includes
only a brief citation or passing reference to the beneficiary's work is not "about" the beneficiary,
relating to the beneficiary's work in the field, as required under this criterion. 8 However, the
beneficiary and the beneficiary's work need not be the only subject ofthe material; published material
that covers a broader topic but includes a substantial discussion of the beneficiary's work in the field
and mentions the beneficiary in connection to the work may be considered material "about" the
beneficiary relating the work. 9 Here, the articles are not about the Beneficiary but regarding the study.
In fact, the Beneficiary is never mentioned, and the articles do not qualify as published material about
him.
'I~----~
Similarly, the Petitioner submitted three articles posted on amazon.science.com about the
I I'
along with the Beneficiary's co-authored article.
The articles never mention the Beneficiary, and the Petitioner did not establish the connection between
the materials or if the Beneficiary was involved with the competition. Regardless, the Petitioner did
not demonstrate that the evidence reflects published material about him relating to his work rather than
about the competition.
For the reasons discussed above, the Petitioner did not provide evidence showing published material
about the Beneficiary. Therefore, we need not determine whether the websites qualify as professional
publications, major trade publications, or major media. 10
Accordingly, the Petitioner did not demonstrate the Beneficiary satisfies this criterion.

The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(5) requires "[e]vidence of the alien's original
scientific, scholarly, or business-related contributions of major significance in the field." Analysis
under this criterion focuses on whether the beneficiary's original work constitutes major, significant
contributions in the field. 11 The Petitioner argues the Beneficiary's eligibility for this criterion based
on the "measurable impact of [the Beneficiary's] publication in JAMA Network Open, a peer­
reviewed journal of national and international renown" and references Altmetric figures and
testimonial letters.
Regarding the claim of publication in a 'journal of national and international renown," the Petitioner
did not establish that articles published in highly ranked journals or from reputable conference
proceedings reflect majorly significant contributions in the field, nor are we persuaded that all articles
appearing in highly esteemed journals are automatically considered to be of major significance in the
8 See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
9 Id.
10 See INS v. Bagamasbad, 429 U.S. 24, 25 (1976) (per curiam) (holding that agencies are not required to make "purely
advisory findings" on issues that are unnecessary to the ultimate decision).
11 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
5
field. 12 The issue for this criterion is not reputation ofthe journal or conference but whether the article
is considered by the field to be ofmajor significance. Moreover, a publication that bears a high ranking
or impact factor reflects the publication's overall citation rate; it does not show an author's influence
or the impact of research on the field or that every article published in a highly ranked journal
inevitably indicates a contribution of major significance. Here, the Petitioner has not established that
publication in a popular or highly ranked journal alone demonstrates a contribution of major
significance in the field.
Regarding the JAMA Network Open article, the Petitioner provided Google Scholar information
reflecting the article received 44 citations and Altmetrics data showing various numbers, such as an
"Altmetric Attention Score of 59" and "[t]his is our high-level measure of quality and quantity of
online attention," "this one has done particularly well and is in the 97th percentile," "[t]his one has
gotten more attention than average, scoring higher than 63% of its peers," "[t]his one has done
particularly well, scoring higher than 95% of its contemporaries," and "[t]his one has gotten more
attention than average, scoring higher than 65% of its contemporaries." However, the Petitioner did
not contextualize the Google Scholar or Altmetrics information to show how these particular figures
establish a contribution of major significance in the field. 13 While the data may indicate that the
Beneficiary's article received some attention, the Petitioner did not demonstrate that these numbers
raise the Beneficiary's article to a contribution of major significance in the field. Without farther
information, including the relevance ofthe Altmetrics statistics and the factors contributing to the data,
the Petitioner did not establish that the Beneficiary's article qualifies as a contribution of major
significance in the field, consistent with this regulatory criterion.
Likewise, the Petitioner asserts that the Beneficiary's "article has been ... featured in national medical
news outlets such as Physician Weekly, and widely disseminated across academic and clinical
networks." Here, the Petitioner did not farther elaborate and explain how the Beneficiary's co­
authored article reported in two publications reflects its status as a contribution of major significance
in the field. The Petitioner did not show that being reported in two publications indicates widespread
commentary or significant attention. 14 For example, the Petitioner did not compare the media
coverage of the Beneficiary's co-authored article to the media coverage of other articles in the
Beneficiary's field that are viewed as contributions of major significance in the field.
Moreover, the Petitioner provided a letter from P-R- who broadly claimed that the Beneficiary
"presented groundbreaking findings that address the pressing issue of time management in healthcare
through novel AI-driven systems" and "[t]his publication has received significant attention, reflected
in an Altmetric score of 59 and extensive media coverage." Likewise, the previously mentioned letter
from T-M- and A-K- generally assert that the Beneficiary's "publications have received dozens of

supra, at M.4(C)(2) (instructing that documentation of original work published in a scholarly journal of distinguished

citations, earned strong Altmetric scores, and been featured in industry media, reflecting broad
influence in the field." However, the letters do not further elaborate and provide detailed information
to support their assertions or to explain their claims. 15 Here, the Petitioner did not demonstrate that
the letters offered on behalf of the Beneficiary show his contributions of major significance in the
field.
Accordingly, the Petitioner did not establish the Beneficiary meets this criterion.

E. Capacity
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(7) requires "[e]vidence that the alien has been
employed in a critical or essential capacity for organizations or establishments that have a
distinguished reputation." The record reflects that the Beneficiary served in a critical or essential
capacity for the Petitioner as its co-founder and chief technology officer. However, the Petitioner did
not show that it possesses a distinguished reputation.
USCIS determines whether the organization or establishment has a distinguished reputation. 16
Relevant factors for evaluating the reputation of an organization or establishment can include the scale
of its customer base, longevity, or relevant media coverage. 17 For a startup business, USCIS may
consider evidence that the business has received significant funding from government entities, venture
capital funds, angel investors, or other such funder commensurate with funding rounds generally
achieved for that startup's stage and industry, as a positive factor regarding its distinguished
reputation.
According to the petition and supporting the petition, the Petitioner was established inl 12025,
approximately two months prior to the filing. The Petitioner did not demonstrate how in only two
months it was able to acquire a distinguished reputation. Moreover, as discussed under the awards
criterion, the Petitioner secured capital venture funding from three investors totaling $250K.
However, the Petitioner did not contextualize the amount of $250K or establish that the amount is
tantamount to significant funding from venture capital funds. Thus, the Petitioner did not show that
its receipt of venture capital funding in the amount of $250K reflects its distinguished reputation.
Moreover, the Petitioner did not offer any other evidence, such as customer base information or
relevant media coverage, to indicate how it differentiates itself from other healthcare artificial
intelligence businesses.
Accordingly, the Petitioner did not demonstrate the Beneficiary fulfills this criterion.
